q: How do you use AI to reduce alert noise and correlate alerts into incidents?
a: I start with the basics, because they remove most noise: deduplicate identical alerts, group by service, cluster and time window, suppress child alerts when a parent dependency is down, and alert on symptoms tied to SLOs rather than on every cause. Then correlation. Topology-aware grouping uses the service dependency graph, so alerts from a database and its callers form one incident. Text and label similarity can cluster alerts that share fields. A model can propose groupings and a short description, while engineers confirm. I measure alerts per incident, pages per on-call shift, the share of actionable pages, and time to acknowledge. Every grouping rule is reviewed after incidents, and feedback buttons mark alerts as useful or noise. I avoid black-box suppression that could hide a real outage, so suppressed alerts stay visible in an audit view, and critical SLO alerts always page.
f: What is parent-child alert suppression?
How do you prove noise actually dropped?
p: Deduplicate, group by service and window, suppress child alerts, and alert on SLO symptoms. Add topology-aware correlation and model-proposed groupings that humans confirm. Measure alerts per incident and actionable pages, and never hide critical alerts.
tip: Say suppressed alerts must stay auditable.

q: How can LLMs help draft postmortems, and what must humans still own?
a: A model can save hours of clerical work. Given the incident timeline from chat, the alert history, deployment records, and ticket updates, it can draft a chronological summary, list impact figures from linked dashboards, extract action items, and propose a first version of the contributing factors. It can also check a draft against a template for missing sections. Humans must still own the analysis. The model does not know what people were thinking at decision points, it can invent plausible causes, and it tends toward neat single root causes when real incidents have several contributing factors. I therefore require every claim to cite a timeline entry, have the incident commander review the facts, and keep the review blameless, with people deciding the lessons and the priorities for follow-up. I also keep sensitive details restricted, and track whether action items get completed, since that is where postmortems create value.
f: Why avoid a single root cause?
How do you keep it blameless?
p: Use a model to assemble the timeline, impact summary, action items and template checks from incident records, with citations. Humans validate facts, analyse contributing factors blamelessly, choose priorities and track the follow-up work.
tip: Say the model drafts, but people own the lessons.

q: How would you build a Kubernetes troubleshooting assistant for developers, and keep it safe?
a: I would build it as a read-only assistant first. It accepts a question such as why a pod is crash looping, and calls a small set of vetted tools: describe pod, recent events, logs of the previous container, resource usage, recent rollouts, and node conditions, all through a service account limited to the user's own namespaces. The model combines the evidence into an explanation with likely causes, for example an out-of-memory kill, a failing readiness probe or an image pull error, and suggests commands the user can run. Safety: no write access by default, outputs scanned for secrets, logs treated as untrusted text, rate limits, and audit logging. If I later allow actions such as restarting a deployment, they need confirmation from the user and run with the user's own permissions. I evaluate on a library of known failure scenarios in a test cluster, checking that the diagnosis is correct and that it asks for more data when evidence is thin.
f: Which tools would you expose first?
How do you test it on known failures?
p: A read-only assistant with vetted tools for describe, events, logs, usage and rollouts under the user's own permissions. It explains likely causes with evidence, treats logs as untrusted, audits use, and is tested on a library of known failure scenarios.
tip: Say read-only first, then confirmed actions with user permissions.

q: Which techniques cut token spend without hurting quality, such as batch APIs, shorter prompts and context pruning?
a: I look at where tokens go before optimising. Typical savings come from several places. Trim prompts: remove verbose instructions and redundant examples, and keep stable text at the start so prompt caching applies. Prune context: retrieve fewer, better chunks, summarise old conversation turns, and drop tool outputs once used. Limit output with maximum length and concise format instructions. Use the cheapest adequate model for each step, and route easy requests to smaller ones. Use batch or asynchronous processing for work that is not urgent, since many providers price batch jobs lower. Avoid unnecessary calls through caching and deduplication, and stop agent loops early. Each change is checked against the evaluation set, because a cheaper prompt that lowers accuracy costs more in rework. I track tokens and cost per task over time, and review the most expensive prompts regularly.
f: How do you verify quality after trimming?
Which requests suit batch processing?
p: Measure first, then trim prompts, prune context, cap output, route to cheaper models, batch non-urgent work and cache repeats. Validate every change against the evaluation set and track cost per task.
tip: Say each saving must pass the evaluation set.

q: How do quantisation and model size choices change the cost of serving, and how do you decide?
a: Cost per token is driven by how many GPUs are needed and how many tokens each can produce. A smaller model, or a quantised one using 8-bit or 4-bit weights, needs less memory, so it can fit on fewer or cheaper GPUs, leaves more room for the KV cache and larger batches, and often decodes faster because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound. The trade-off is potential quality loss, which varies by task: extraction and classification often tolerate it well, while complex reasoning or code may not. I decide empirically. I run the evaluation set on candidates, such as the full-precision model, an 8-bit version and a smaller model, and benchmark throughput at my latency target. Then I compute cost per thousand successful tasks, not just cost per token. I also consider operational factors: kernel support on my GPUs, ease of upgrades, and monitoring quality after changes in production.
f: Why is decoding memory-bandwidth bound?
What is cost per successful task?
p: Smaller or quantised models need fewer GPUs and leave more KV cache room, raising throughput. Compare full precision, quantised and smaller models on the evaluation set and benchmarks, and decide by cost per successful task.
tip: Say you compare cost per successful task, not per token.

q: How do you set up human review and labelling for evaluating an AI feature?
a: Human labels are the ground truth that automated metrics are checked against, so the process matters. I define clear guidelines with a rubric, examples of each score, and rules for edge cases, then pilot with a few reviewers and refine ambiguous instructions. I choose reviewers with the right expertise, such as support leads or engineers, and measure agreement between them, for example with Cohen's kappa; low agreement signals unclear criteria rather than bad reviewers. I sample cases deliberately: a random set for overall quality, plus failures, low-confidence outputs and important segments. Tooling should show the full context, hide model identity when comparing, and capture reasons for scores. I protect sensitive data by redacting and restricting access. Labels are versioned and used to calibrate LLM judges and to grow the regression set. Review is ongoing, with a small weekly sample to detect drift, because labelling every output is not realistic.
f: What does low reviewer agreement tell you?
How do you sample cases to review?
p: Write a rubric with examples, pilot it, use qualified reviewers, measure agreement, sample randomly and by risk, blind comparisons, protect data, version labels and use them to calibrate automated judges and grow regression sets.
tip: Say low agreement usually means an unclear rubric.

q: What is benchmark contamination and how do you avoid fooling yourself with evaluation results?
a: Contamination means the evaluation data, or something very similar, was seen by the model during training, so scores overstate real ability. Public benchmarks are especially exposed. For my own evaluation I keep a private test set built from real, recent traffic and domain cases, never published or used in prompts or fine-tuning, and I keep a separate development set for tuning so I do not overfit to the test set. I check overlap between fine-tuning data and test data with deduplication. Other traps include data leakage through retrieval of the answer key, tuning prompts against the same examples used to report results, small sample sizes with no confidence intervals, and only reporting aggregates that hide failures in important segments. I report uncertainty, break results down by category, refresh the test set periodically, and confirm gains with online experiments, since offline numbers do not always carry over to real users.
f: How do you detect overlap with training data?
Why keep a separate dev set?
p: Contamination inflates scores when test data was seen in training. Use private, recent test sets separate from development data, deduplicate against fine-tuning data, report confidence intervals and segment results, refresh sets and confirm with online tests.
tip: Say report confidence intervals and per-segment results.

q: How do you evaluate guardrails, including false positives and false negatives?
a: A guardrail is a classifier, so I evaluate it as one. I build a labelled set with two sides: harmful or policy-violating inputs and outputs that should be blocked, such as injection attempts, personal data and unsafe requests, and benign but similar-looking cases that should pass. I then measure the false negative rate, which is risk getting through, and the false positive rate, which blocks legitimate users and harms the experience. I look at both by category and at different thresholds to choose an operating point matched to the risk: strict for high-severity categories, more lenient elsewhere. I test against adversarial variants, such as paraphrases, encodings and other languages. I also measure latency added and cost. In production, I log triggers, sample blocked and allowed cases for review, and track rates over time to catch drift. The set is refreshed with new attacks found by red teaming and with real false positives reported by users.
f: How do you choose a threshold?
Why test other languages?
p: Treat the guardrail as a classifier: a labelled set with harmful and benign look-alike cases, measure false negatives and positives per category and threshold, test adversarial variants, track latency, review samples in production and refresh the set.
tip: Say you measure both blocked-good and missed-bad.

q: How does the position of information in a long prompt affect results, and how do you structure long contexts?
a: Models do not use all parts of a long context equally well. Information buried in the middle is often used less reliably than information at the beginning or the end, and irrelevant text can distract the model. I structure long prompts deliberately. Put stable instructions first, which also helps caching. Place the documents in clearly delimited sections with identifiers, and put the specific question or task after the documents, sometimes repeating key constraints at the end. Order retrieved passages by relevance and keep only what is needed, since more context is not always better. For multi-document work, ask the model to quote relevant passages first and then answer from them, which improves grounding. I test with questions whose answers sit at different positions in the context, using my own models and data, because behaviour varies by model. If results degrade, I shorten the context, summarise in stages, or split the task across calls.
f: What is the lost-in-the-middle effect?
How do you test position sensitivity?
p: Put stable instructions first, delimit documents with identifiers, place the question after the material, order by relevance, ask for quotes before answers and trim context. Test answers at different positions and split tasks if quality degrades.
tip: Say you test answer position on your own model.

q: How do you handle multilingual users in prompts and evaluation?
a: I first learn which languages matter and how well the model performs in each, because quality varies, often lower for less common languages, and tokenisation makes non-English text cost more tokens. Design choices: instruct the model to reply in the user's language, keep system instructions in one language the team can maintain, and avoid translating idioms in few-shot examples carelessly. Retrieval needs a multilingual embedding model, or translation before indexing, and I test cross-language retrieval. For evaluation, I build test sets per language with native-speaking reviewers, since machine translated test sets hide errors, and report results per language rather than as an average. Guardrails also need testing in each language, because injection and safety filters can be weaker outside English. Finally, I watch cost and latency per language, and use fallbacks, for example a stronger model for languages where the primary model is weak.
f: Why do non-English prompts cost more?
How do you test retrieval across languages?
p: Measure per-language quality, instruct replies in the user's language, use multilingual embeddings, build native-reviewed test sets, evaluate guardrails per language and track token cost, with stronger-model fallbacks where needed.
tip: Say report per-language results, not one average.

q: How do you choose and upgrade an embedding model without breaking a RAG system?
a: I choose by testing on my own data, not only public leaderboards: build a retrieval evaluation set of real questions with known relevant documents, then compare candidate models on recall at k and ranking quality, together with dimensions, maximum input length, language support, latency, cost and licence. Dimensions affect storage and search speed. Upgrading is disruptive, because vectors from different models are not compatible, so I treat it as a migration. Build a new index in parallel with the new model, run the evaluation on both, shadow production queries against the new index to compare results, then switch traffic gradually behind a flag and keep the old index for rollback. Queries and documents must use the same model and version, so I store the model name and version with each vector. The re-embedding cost for the corpus is estimated in advance, and I limit upgrades to cases where measured gains justify them.
f: Why can you not mix vectors from two models?
How do you estimate re-embedding cost?
p: Choose by recall and ranking on your own evaluation set plus dimensions, length, language, cost and licence. Upgrade as a migration: build a parallel index, shadow queries, switch gradually, store the model version with vectors and keep rollback.
cmds: SELECT embedding_model, count(*) FROM chunks GROUP BY 1;
tip: Say vectors from different models are incompatible, so upgrades are migrations.

q: How do you design multi-tenant RAG so tenants never see each other's data?
a: Isolation must be enforced in the retrieval layer, not left to the prompt. There are three common designs. A separate index or collection per tenant gives the strongest isolation and simple deletion, at the cost of operational overhead with many tenants. A shared index with a mandatory tenant filter on every query is cheaper, but a bug in filter handling can leak data, so the filter must be applied by a server-side layer the application cannot skip. A hybrid places large or sensitive tenants in dedicated indexes and small ones in shared ones. Beyond tenants, document-level permissions are checked at query time. Other safeguards include per-tenant encryption keys where required, caches scoped by tenant, logs separated and access controlled, and tests that attempt cross-tenant queries and expect empty results. Deletion and offboarding procedures must remove vectors, source copies and caches, and be verifiable.
f: When would you prefer an index per tenant?
How do you test for cross-tenant leakage?
p: Enforce isolation in retrieval: per-tenant indexes for strongest separation, or a shared index with a server-enforced tenant filter, or a hybrid. Add document-level permissions, scoped caches and logs, tests for cross-tenant queries and verifiable deletion.
cmds: python leak_test.py --tenant A --query "tenant B salary data" --expect-empty
tip: Say the tenant filter must be server-enforced.

q: Where should human approval sit in an agent workflow, and how do you design it so people do not just click approve?
a: I place approval on actions that are irreversible, costly, external-facing or high privilege, such as sending customer email, changing production, spending money or deleting data. Low-risk reads proceed automatically so the agent remains useful. To prevent approval fatigue, I keep the number of prompts low by grouping related steps into a plan that is approved once, with clear scope and limits. The request shows what will happen in plain language: the exact action, target, parameters, expected effect and a diff or preview where possible, plus the evidence the agent used. The default is deny, with timeouts that fail safe. Approvers need authority matching the action, and their decisions are logged with the agent's reasoning. I measure the approval rate and time; an approval rate near 100 percent suggests either the checks are unnecessary or people are rubber-stamping, and I adjust. Over time, well-understood actions can move to automatic within limits.
f: What does approval fatigue look like?
Which actions can become automatic later?
p: Require approval for irreversible, costly, external or privileged actions, group steps into approved plans, show exact actions with previews and evidence, default to deny, log decisions, and track approval rates to detect rubber-stamping.
tip: Say show a diff or preview, not a vague yes or no.

q: How do you make agent actions reliable with retries, idempotency and failure recovery?
a: Agents call tools over networks and the model itself can repeat or mis-order steps, so I use ordinary distributed systems discipline. Tool calls get timeouts and bounded retries with backoff and jitter, and distinguish transient errors from permanent ones, returning clear error messages the model can act on. Write operations are idempotent: an idempotency key per intended action means a repeated call does not create a duplicate ticket or double charge. Long tasks checkpoint their state after each step, so a crash resumes from the last checkpoint rather than restarting or repeating completed side effects. Where multiple steps must succeed together, I design compensating actions or use a workflow engine with sagas. Loops are bounded by maximum steps, tokens and time, with detection of repeated identical calls. On unrecoverable failure, the agent stops, reports what was done and what remains, and hands over to a human. I test with injected failures to confirm these paths work.
f: What is an idempotency key?
How do you inject failures for testing?
p: Use timeouts, bounded retries with backoff, idempotency keys for writes, checkpoints after each step, compensating actions for multi-step changes, bounded loops and a clear handoff on failure. Test with injected faults.
tip: Say treat tool calls like any unreliable network call.

q: How do you choose between building an agent with a framework and writing a thin custom loop?
a: I decide based on how much the framework gives me versus the control and clarity I lose. Frameworks provide ready patterns: tool calling loops, memory, tracing integrations, multi-agent graphs, and connectors, which speeds up prototypes and gives a shared vocabulary. The costs are abstraction layers that obscure what is sent to the model, fast-changing interfaces, harder debugging, and dependency risk. A thin custom loop is often only a few dozen lines around the model API: send messages, execute requested tools, append results, stop on a condition. It is transparent, easy to test, and easy to add limits, logging and permissions to. My usual approach is to prototype in whichever is fastest, then for production keep the core loop simple and owned by us, using libraries for specific needs such as tracing, schema validation or protocol support like MCP. Whatever I choose, I keep tool definitions, prompts and evaluations independent of the framework to limit lock-in.
f: What would push you toward a framework?
How do you avoid lock-in?
p: Frameworks speed up prototypes but add abstraction, churn and debugging cost. A thin owned loop is transparent and easy to control. Prototype quickly, keep the production core simple, use libraries selectively and keep tools, prompts and evaluations portable.
cmds: while not done: resp = llm(messages, tools); run_tools(resp); messages.append(results)
tip: Say keep tools, prompts and evals framework-independent.

q: How do you serve many fine-tuned variants efficiently with LoRA adapters?
a: Fine-tuning a full copy of the model per customer or task wastes GPU memory, because each copy holds billions of weights. LoRA produces small adapter weights, usually megabytes, that modify a shared base model. Serving engines such as vLLM can hold one base model on the GPU and load many adapters, applying the right adapter per request, even mixing different adapters in the same batch. This lets a few GPUs serve dozens or hundreds of variants. The practical points are: adapters are stored in a registry with versions and loaded on demand with an LRU cache, requests specify the adapter name, and capacity planning covers the number of adapters kept resident and the extra latency when one must load. Adapter quality is evaluated separately per variant. There is a small throughput cost compared with a merged model, so a very high-traffic variant may be merged and served on its own. Access control must stop one tenant using another's adapter.
f: What is the trade-off with merging adapters?
How do you control which tenant can load which adapter?
p: Keep one base model on the GPU and apply small LoRA adapters per request, loaded on demand from a versioned registry with caching. This serves many variants cheaply; merge very busy variants, evaluate each, and enforce adapter access control.
tip: Say one base model, many small adapters.

q: What is prefix caching, and how can KV cache offloading improve serving efficiency?
a: Many requests share a long prefix, such as the system prompt, tool definitions or a shared document. Prefix caching stores the computed key-value cache for that prefix, so later requests reuse it instead of repeating the prefill computation. This cuts time to first token and GPU work, particularly for chat with long history and for RAG with repeated context. To benefit, prompts must keep the shared part identical and at the start, and routing should send related requests to the same replica, using cache-aware or session-affinity routing. The KV cache is large and GPU memory limited, so offloading moves less-used blocks to CPU memory or fast storage and brings them back when needed, trading some latency for the ability to hold more context and sessions. The costs are extra transfer time and complexity. I monitor cache hit rate, time to first token, and memory use, and test that eviction does not harm tail latency.
f: How does routing affect cache hit rate?
When does offloading hurt latency?
p: Prefix caching reuses KV cache for shared prompt prefixes, cutting prefill time and cost, if prompts are stable at the start and routing is cache-aware. Offloading moves cold KV blocks to CPU or storage to hold more sessions, at some latency cost.
tip: Say keep shared text identical and at the start of prompts.

q: How do you load test and capacity-plan an LLM service before launch?
a: I use realistic workloads, because LLM load depends on prompt and output lengths, not only request counts. First, collect or synthesise a request distribution from real or expected traffic: input tokens, output tokens, concurrency, and the share of cached prefixes. Then run a load generator that ramps the request rate in steps and records time to first token, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency percentiles, throughput in tokens per second, error rate, queue depth, GPU utilisation and KV cache usage. The result is a curve showing the maximum rate per replica that still meets the latency SLO, which is the capacity number to plan with, with headroom of perhaps 30 percent for spikes and failures. I also test overload behaviour to confirm load shedding and autoscaling work, test failure of a replica, and repeat after each major model or engine change. Findings feed into autoscaling targets, quotas and the cost model.
f: Why test with realistic length distributions?
What headroom do you keep?
p: Use realistic prompt and output length distributions, ramp load in steps, record TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, errors and GPU and KV cache use, find the rate per replica that meets the SLO, add headroom, test overload and failures, and repeat after changes.
tip: Say capacity is the highest rate that still meets the latency SLO.
